intro_en:
The Israel National Trail continues southward, with desert landscapes and fine views over the Arava and the Edom Mountains.

To the previous segment: Shizafon Junction – Shaharut (50)
 Be'er Milhan – Timna (52)
character_en: Walking through exposed desert landscape, crossing low hills and channels.
transport_en: At the starting point: the community of Shaharut (low frequency)
important_en: The trail does not pass by the community of Shaharut. You can sleep and stock up on drinking water at the segment's starting point at Khan Shaharut. Food can be obtained by a Shufersal Online delivery, which arrives at Shaharut several times a week.
Be'er Milhan can be reached by vehicle only with a 4x4.
description_en:
The Israel National Trail heads south-west from the Shaharut access road and climbs a low spur. From the top of the spur a view opens westward over a broad plain, which the Israel National Trail crosses along with the upper tributaries of Nahal Isaron.
After an easy climb up the southern side of the channel, the trail turns south. North of the turn you can see the northern dry waterfall of Nahal Isaron, and below the trail the wide channel of the stream can be seen.
A red-marked trail descends into the channel, to Gev Isaron, which lies below the southern dry waterfall of Nahal Isaron. It is recommended to go down to the gev (rock pool), a beautiful spot that fills with floodwater in good winters and allows a dip.
After a short walk on the Israel National Trail we reach a fine lookout above the waterfall and the pool. Take care!
From the lookout, the trail continues south up the stream channel. Beside the way are several large acacia trees. These are Negev acacias – a relatively rare species of acacia that prefers the higher, colder areas. A simple identification sign: the fruit is a sickle- or crescent-shaped pod, but it does not twist into a spiral. The two more common acacia species – the umbrella thorn acacia and the twisted acacia – are met along the Israel National Trail in the Judean Desert, the Negev and the Arava.
We continue through gentle terrain up the tributaries of Nahal Isaron, to a point above Nahal Zugan. The trail descends through the remains of an ancient ascent to the channel of Nahal Zugan and crosses it southward. After the crossing, the trail climbs to the ridge to the south.
We continue a stretch south along the watershed between the streams draining west to the Uvda Valley and the streams Yotvata and Argaman, which descend east to the Arava. Now and then a "window" opens eastward, to the Arava and the high ridge of the Edom Mountains beyond it. On the Israeli side a pale, conical mountain stands out above its surroundings – Mount Argaman.
In this section, clusters of "bulbus" stones appear beside the trail – rounded, slightly flattened rocks. The bulbus stones were formed long ago on the floor of an ancient sea. They developed through a process of concentric crystallization around some nucleus, which creates the distinctive shape of the bulbus.
After meeting a green-marked trail arriving from the east, the Israel National Trail turns south-west, "stitching" (climbing and descending) across several channels and spurs.
On meeting Nahal Milhan, the Israel National Trail turns sharply south-east with a blue-marked dirt road. To reach the end point of the segment at Be'er Milhan and the campsite, we continue west with the blue road for a few hundred meters.
Be'er Milhan is a well of brackish water unfit for drinking. The well was dug and lined with concrete by the British to provide a permanent water source for the Bedouin herds. Nearby, another well is marked, Be'er Matak – which we will not find on the ground, since it was neglected and became blocked over the years.
Points of interest: Gev Isaron, which may be full after rain. Be'er Milhan.
